title: Mud and Adobe
objective: After this level you can explain why thick earth walls suit hot places.
summary: Taos Pueblo's adobe is earth, water and straw, never fired. Thick earth walls store heat, so rooms peak hours later. Water is adobe's enemy, so walls are replastered with mud.

cards.headline: Taos Pueblo's earth homes rose between about 1000 and 1450 CE.
cards.body: They're the multi-storied adobe homes of the people of Taos Pueblo in northern New Mexico, whose native language is Tiwa. Each home is owned by a family, which keeps it up in the traditional way, and the Pueblo has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992. Mud isn't a lesser material. In the right climate, it's the smart one.

cards.headline: Earth, water, straw
cards.body: Adobe is earth mixed with water and straw, either poured into forms or shaped into sun-dried bricks. Level 1's timeline started here: sun-dried mud brick is one of the first building materials. The straw doesn't make the bricks stronger, but it helps them shrink evenly as they dry. At Taos, big timbers called vigas, hauled down from the mountain forests, hold up the roof of each story.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing here, make it this: a heavy wall makes the heat arrive late.

cards.headline: A wall that stores heat
cards.body: Heavy walls have high thermal mass: they can store a lot of heat. When the midday sun beats on a thick earth wall, the heat soaks in slowly, so the room inside reaches its peak a few hours after the air outside. The effect is strongest where days and nights differ most in temperature. Here's an analogy: the wall works like a sponge for heat, soaking it up slowly and letting it go slowly.

cards.fact: Water is adobe's great enemy.
cards.context: Adobe is never fired in a kiln, so it never permanently hardens. It swells and shrinks with its water content, and the wetter it gets, the weaker it is. So adobe buildings last by shedding water and being cared for. At Taos, the outside walls are kept up by replastering them with thick layers of mud and straw. The plaster bonds so well because it's made of the same stuff as the wall.

title: Houses on Stilts
objective: After this level you can explain why some houses stand on stilts.
summary: Rumah panggung on the Musi River stand 1 to 2 m up so floods flow beneath. Alpine pile houses date from about 5000 to 500 BC. Every stilt is a post in compression.

cards.headline: Some of Europe's oldest villages stood on stilts.
cards.body: Around the Alps, from about 5000 to 500 BC, people built wooden houses on piles in or near water: on lakes, on river banks and in bogs. Why would anyone lift a house off the ground? A river community in Indonesia still gives the answer.

cards.headline: Let the flood pass underneath
cards.body: Along the Musi River in South Sumatra, communities build traditional stilt houses called rumah panggung. Raised about 1 to 2 m, they stay safe when floodwater reaches an adult's knees or waist, because the water flows under the floor instead of through the living room. The open space below also lets in air and light, cutting the damp that rots wooden houses. One move, two problems solved.

cards.headline: Standing on legs
cards.body: Stilts are Level 2's load path made visible. The whole house, and everyone in it, pushes down through the posts into the ground, so every stilt is in compression, like any post carrying weight. The Alpine builders planted theirs firmly: they burned each pile's end to a point, drove it deep into the mud, packed heavy stones around it and laid a platform of tree trunks and branches on top.

cards.fact: Archaeologists still debate where the Alpine pile houses stood.
cards.context: In the mid-1800s, the Swiss archaeologist Ferdinand Keller argued they stood on platforms out over the lake water. Researchers now think they may have been built over swampy shore instead. Either way, the wet ground preserved their wood so well that 111 sites in six countries became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.

title: Roman Homes
objective: After this level you can describe Roman houses and apartment blocks.
summary: The rich Roman domus opened to the sky through its atrium. Everyone else lived in insulae: brick-and-concrete blocks of five or more stories, with less water higher up.

cards.headline: In the Roman Empire's great cities, a house of your own was for the rich.
cards.body: Crowding meant that by early imperial times, the private house had given way to the insula, a shared apartment block, for everyone but the very wealthy. So there were two ways to live in Rome: the rich family's domus, and everyone else's insula.

cards.headline: A house around a hole in the roof
cards.body: A wealthy Roman's house centered on the atrium, an open central court. Above it, an opening in the roof, the compluvium, let the rain in. Below it, a marble basin, the impluvium, caught the water. Larger houses added a colonnaded court farther in, the peristyle, with the family's private rooms clustered around it. Rain, delivered to the living room on purpose.

cards.headline: An island of apartments
cards.body: Insula is Latin for "island": a block rising from the street. Insulae were built of brick covered with concrete and were often five or more stories high, despite a height limit of about 21 m under the emperor Augustus. At street level were workshops and shops. Above them, homes reached by a shared staircase, taking light and air from the street and an inner court.

cards.fact: In an insula, the higher you lived, the harder life got.
cards.context: Piped water reached only the lower apartments, so people upstairs had to use public facilities. Many insulae were cheaply built, and collapse and fire were constant dangers. Picture carrying every bucket of water up five flights, in a building that might burn. Nobody was bragging about the penthouse.

title: Timber Frames
objective: After this level you can explain building with wood, from log cabins to half-timbered towns.
summary: Log houses stack whole trees crossed at the corners, from Vitruvius's Colchians to New Sweden (1638). In timber frames the frame carries the load; wattle and daub fills in.

cards.headline: About 2,000 years ago, Vitruvius described a log house.
cards.body: Among the Colchians, where forests were plentiful, he wrote, people laid whole trees flat, crossed them at the corners, and stacked them up into walls around a dwelling, filling the gaps with chips and mud. Colchis lay at the eastern end of the Black Sea, in what is now western Georgia. Wood can make a house two ways: stack it, or frame it.

cards.headline: Stack the trees
cards.body: A log cabin is that method in its simplest form: four log walls joined at the corners into one room, which builders called a pen. Scandinavians brought the log cabin to America when they settled New Sweden, around Delaware Bay, in 1638. Swedish builders stuffed the gaps with chinking, such as moss and clay. One Finnish-built cabin of 1638 to 1643, the Nothnagle Log House in New Jersey, is still standing.

cards.headline: Or build a skeleton
cards.body: Timber-framed houses do the opposite. In a medieval timber-framed building, the frame of timbers is the load-bearing structure, and the spaces between the timbers only need filling to keep the weather out. A common filling was wattle and daub: small timbers woven into a lattice, then daubed with mud, dung, water and straw. Sound familiar? It's Level 8's frame building, where the skeleton carries the floors and the walls hold only themselves.

cards.fact: In colonial America, the two ways of building met.
cards.context: Scandinavian settlers brought log building to New Sweden in 1638. English settlers preferred frame construction and didn't take up log building until the 18th century. Later, Welsh and Scots-Irish settlers carried the log cabin inland to the western frontier. Same forests, different traditions: people built the way they had learned back home.

title: Row Houses and Apartments
objective: After this level you can explain how cities stacked homes to save space.
summary: Row houses share side walls; Bath's Royal Crescent put 30 behind one palace front. Crowding pushed cities up into apartments, and Paris flats got smaller higher up.

cards.headline: Bath's Royal Crescent looks like one palace. It's 30 houses.
cards.body: John Wood the Younger designed it, and building began in 1767: a great curve of attached townhouses behind one unified front. Cities have two ways to fit more homes onto less land. Line them up, or stack them.

cards.headline: Line them up
cards.body: A row house is one of a series of houses joined by shared side walls into one continuous group. The Royal Crescent's unified, palace-like front was the first such design in English town architecture. Behind it, each original buyer bought a length of the front and had their own architect build the house to order, so the backs don't match. All the grandeur is on the front; the backs are a jumble.

cards.headline: Stack them up
cards.body: When crowding and rising land values make one-family houses impractical, cities build up instead, and the apartment house grows in importance. Remember Level 46? In the Roman Empire's crowded great cities, the private house had given way to the insula for all but the very wealthy. Later cities faced the same squeeze with the same answer: more floors.

cards.fact: In old Paris, money lived downstairs.
cards.context: In a typical 19th-century Paris apartment building of four or five stories, the apartments got smaller with each story up, and so did the tenants' means. Rome's insulae had a similar ladder: piped water reached only the lower apartments. In both cities, climbing the stairs meant climbing down the social ladder.

title: The Modern House
objective: After this level you can explain open plans and big windows.
summary: The 1924 Rietveld Schröder House slid open by day and closed into three rooms at night. The Eameses built their 1949 home from catalog parts, its steel frame up in 16 hours.

cards.headline: In 1924, a house in Utrecht let you open a corner into thin air.
cards.body: Truus Schröder asked the furniture designer Gerrit Rietveld to design her new home, and she played an important part in the design herself. On its upper floor, both panes of the corner window swing open, and the corner simply disappears. This house set out to open things up: rooms, walls, even corners.

cards.headline: Walls that slide away
cards.body: The Schröders' upper floor was one open space by day. In the evening, the family used sliding walls to split it into three separate rooms. Call it an open plan with an off switch. The house, designed in 1924 and lived in until 1985, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

cards.headline: A house from a catalog
cards.body: In 1949, Charles and Ray Eames built their own home from prefabricated parts ordered out of industrial and commercial catalogs. Construction began in February, and after 16 hours the foundation and steel frame were complete. They moved in on Christmas Eve and lived there for the rest of their lives. Level 8's Crystal Palace pulled the same trick: factory-made parts, put up fast.

cards.fact: A steel frame frees the walls.
cards.context: Remember Level 8: once a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, the outer wall bears only its own weight and hangs on the frame. The Eames House's steel frame was up within 16 hours, so its walls never had to carry the floors: the frame did. And Level 8 showed where that leads: a wall that carries only itself can be thin, even glass.

title: Milestone: How People Build
objective: After this level you can connect materials, climate and purpose into one picture of architecture.
summary: Rudofsky's 1964 MoMA show celebrated architecture without architects. Snow, earth, felt, stilts and timber each answer a climate with Chapter 1's physics.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. So who designed all these homes?
cards.body: Igloos, gers, adobe pueblos, stilt houses: most of this chapter's homes are what ICOMOS calls vernacular building, "the traditional and natural way by which communities house themselves." In 1964, an architect put that idea on the walls of a famous museum.

cards.headline: Architecture Without Architects
cards.body: That was the title of an exhibition at New York's Museum of Modern Art, opening in November 1964. Its director, the architect and engineer Bernard Rudofsky, called his subject non-pedigreed architecture: old, sometimes ancient building traditions evolved and upheld by ordinary people. Level 1 said architects design and builders build. Rudofsky's point: whole communities can do both.

title: Bridges
objective: After this level you can explain the main kinds of bridge.
summary: Beam bridges bend and arch bridges push, while suspension decks hang from curved cables and cable-stayed decks from straight ones. The Forth Bridge (1890) balances on three steel cantilevers.

cards.headline: In 1887, two engineers turned themselves into a bridge.
cards.body: John Fowler and Benjamin Baker sat side by side with their arms held out, and between them sat the engineer Kaichi Watanabe, suspended in the middle. They were showing how their bridge over Scotland's Firth of Forth would work. Every bridge answers the same question: how do you carry weight across a gap? Here are the main answers.

cards.headline: Beams and arches, taken outdoors
cards.body: The two oldest answers come straight from Chapter 1. A beam bridge carries weight by bending: squeezed on top, stretched underneath, just like Level 3's lintel. An arch bridge carries weight mainly by squeezing, in compression, so it needs strong foundations to take its push, Level 4's thrust. A plank over a stream is a beam bridge. A stone curve over a river is an arch.

cards.headline: Two ways to hang a road
cards.body: For longer spans, engineers hang the road. In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from curved cables in tension, which carry the load to towers and to anchorages at each end. Remember Level 10's hanging chain? That's the cable. A cable-stayed bridge skips the big curve: nearly straight diagonal cables run from the deck directly to the towers. France's Millau Viaduct, opened in 2004, is one, strung across the whole Tarn valley by architect Norman Foster and engineer Michel Virlogeux.

cards.fact: The Forth Bridge (1890) balances on three giant cantilevers.
cards.context: A cantilever is a beam supported at one end only, like a diving board. Fowler and Baker's bridge joins three cantilevers with two suspended spans, and it was the world's first major steel structure. In their 1887 human model, Watanabe sat where a suspended span goes, the men's arms were in tension and their sticks in compression. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.

title: The Brooklyn Bridge
objective: After this level you can explain how the Brooklyn Bridge was built.
summary: Caissons dug out under compressed air gave workers the bends. John Roebling designed the bridge; Washington directed it by telescope, Emily relayed his orders. It opened in 1883 on steel cables.

cards.headline: The Brooklyn Bridge's chief engineer watched it rise through a telescope.
cards.body: From his bedroom window in Brooklyn, Washington Roebling followed work he could no longer visit. How did the man in charge end up stuck at home? The answer starts at the bottom of the East River.

cards.headline: Digging from inside a box
cards.body: The bridge's two towers stand on caissons: huge bottomless boxes sunk to the riverbed. Compressed air was pumped in to keep the water out, and inside, workers dug away the sediment so the box sank deeper. Then the caissons were filled with concrete to become the towers' foundations. It's like pushing an upside-down cup into a bath: the trapped air keeps the inside dry.

cards.headline: The bends, and a family business
cards.body: Coming up too fast from that pressurized air let nitrogen bubbles form in the workers' blood: caisson disease, now called the bends. In 1872 it struck Washington Roebling. He had taken over from his father, John A. Roebling, the bridge's designer, who died of tetanus in 1869 after a ferry crushed his toes. So Washington watched through his telescope, and his wife, Emily Warren Roebling, carried his directions to the engineers on the bridge.

cards.fact: 1883: the longest span in the world, hung on steel.
cards.context: The bridge opened on May 24, 1883. Its 486-meter (1,595-foot) main span was the longest in the world when it opened, and it was the first bridge to use steel for its cable wire. It's a suspension bridge, so that deck hangs from cables in tension. Emily Roebling rode in the first carriage across, carrying a rooster as a symbol of victory.

title: The Eiffel Tower
objective: After this level you can explain how the Eiffel Tower was built and why people first hated it.
summary: Engineers Koechlin and Nouguier conceived it, Sauvestre dressed it, artists called it monstrous. About 18,000 prefabricated iron pieces rose by 1889, and radio saved it from demolition.

cards.headline: In 1887, Paris's leading artists protested against a tower that barely existed.
cards.body: On February 14, 1887, the newspaper Le Temps printed their protest against "the useless and monstrous Eiffel Tower". The signers included the architect Charles Garnier and the composer Charles Gounod. So why was it built, how did it go up, and how did something so hated survive?

cards.headline: An engineers' sketch, dressed by an architect
cards.body: The idea came in 1884 from two engineers in Gustave Eiffel's company, Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier: a gigantic metal pylon 300 meters tall. To make it more acceptable to the public, the architect Stephen Sauvestre added the great decorative arches between its feet, glass-walled rooms and stone pedestals. The tower was built for Paris's 1889 International Exposition, marking 100 years since the French Revolution.

cards.headline: A kit of 18,000 pieces
cards.body: Each of the tower's roughly 18,000 wrought-iron pieces was designed in advance, traced to a tenth of a millimeter, and pre-assembled into sections about 5 meters long before going up. Some 2.5 million rivets hold them together, and the whole tower rose in about two years, from 1887 to 1889. It's Level 8's Crystal Palace trick, prefabricated parts, carried 300 meters into the sky.

cards.headline: Saved by being useful
cards.body: Eiffel's permit ran for only 20 years, so after 1909 the tower's future was uncertain. His answer was to make it useful. In 1898 the first wireless telegraph trials linked the tower with the Panthéon, and its value for radio won Eiffel a 70-year extension starting in 1910. Level 1's Vitruvius would approve: commodity, being useful to people, rescued the building critics said had no delight.

title: Tunnels
objective: After this level you can explain how tunnels are dug through rock and under water.
summary: Through rock, tunnellers drill, blast and clear in a cycle. Under water, prefabricated tubes are floated out and sunk into a trench. Either way, a tunnel is an arch that goes all the way round.

cards.headline: Some tunnels under the sea were built in a factory on land.
cards.body: The Øresund Tunnel between Denmark and Sweden is made of 20 giant elements, manufactured at a tunnel factory in Denmark and then sunk into place. How you build a tunnel depends on what's in the way: hard rock or open water.

cards.headline: Through rock: drill, blast, repeat
cards.body: In hard rock, tunnellers work in a cycle. Drill holes into the rock face, load them with explosives, blast, clear the fumes, haul away the broken rock (called muck), and start again. The Mont Cenis Tunnel through the Alps (1857-71) pioneered rail-mounted drill carriages and compressed-air drills to speed up the drilling. A drill-and-blast tunnel moves forward one blast at a time.

cards.headline: Under water: sink a tube
cards.body: Under a river or strait, engineers can build the tunnel first and bury it after. In an immersed-tube tunnel, long prefabricated sections are floated to the site, sunk into a trench dredged in the bottom, and covered over. The Detroit River Railroad Tunnel (1906-10) was the first, and since 1950 it has been the preferred way to tunnel under water. Each Øresund element weighs 55,000 tons, and a tunnel was chosen there so planes at Copenhagen Airport and big ships could pass freely.

mascot.line: A bridge arch holds up a road. A tunnel arch holds up a mountain. Same trick, bigger audience.

cards.headline: An arch that goes all the way round
cards.body: Once it's open, a tunnel has one job: not getting crushed. The ground presses on it from every side, not just from above. So a tunnel's basic shape is a continuous arch: the curve of Level 4, carried all the way round. Just as an arch's wedges squeeze together under weight, a tunnel's ring is pressed together by the ground around it.

title: Dams
objective: After this level you can explain how dams hold back so much water.
summary: Water pushes harder with depth, so dams thicken at the base. Gravity dams use weight, arch dams push into valley sides, embankments are earth or rock. Hoover Dam rose in cooled columns.

cards.headline: Poured in one go, Hoover Dam would have taken 125 years to cool.
cards.body: Setting concrete gives off heat. Engineers calculated that a single giant pour would have stayed hot for 125 years, and the stresses would have cracked the dam. That was one problem. The first was bigger: how does a wall of concrete hold back a whole lake?

cards.headline: Deeper water pushes harder
cards.body: Water pressure increases with depth. Poke two holes in a full plastic bottle and water squirts faster from the lower one. So a dam must be thickest at the bottom, where the push is greatest. Hoover Dam is 660 feet thick at its base and just 45 feet at its crest: less a wall than a wedge.

cards.headline: Built in blocks, chilled with pipes
cards.body: Hoover Dam, finished in 1936, is an arch-gravity dam: its weight and its arch action both carry the water. To beat the heat, it went up as separate columns rising in five-foot lifts. Steel pipes inside the concrete carried river water, then chilled water from a refrigeration plant. After 582 miles of pipe, the cooling was done by March 1935.

title: Canals
objective: After this level you can explain the Suez and Panama canals.
summary: Suez is an open cut with no locks. De Lesseps's sea-level plan failed at Panama. The US built locks up to Gatun Lake, fought the mosquitoes under Gorgas, and opened the canal in 1914.

cards.headline: The man behind the Suez Canal tried the same plan in Panama, and it failed.
cards.body: Ferdinand de Lesseps had led the building of the Suez Canal, opened in 1869. In 1881 his company began a canal across Panama. By 1889 it had collapsed. Why did a plan that worked in Egypt fail in Central America?

cards.headline: Suez: a ditch between two seas
cards.body: The Suez Canal is an open cut with no locks. It links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, running through lakes along the way such as Lake Timsah and the Bitter Lakes. Ships simply sail through. De Lesseps wanted Panama the same way: a sea-level canal. He refused to adopt a plan with locks.

mascot.line: Can't dig the hill away? Make the ships climb it instead.

cards.headline: Panama: a staircase for ships
cards.body: When the United States took over in 1904, its engineers judged that digging all the way down to sea level would take too long and cost too much. So they built locks. A series of three locks lifts ships 85 feet (26 meters) to Gatun Lake, made by damming the Chagres River. The locks fill by gravity, without pumps: the lake's own water does the lifting.

cards.headline: The real enemy was a mosquito
cards.body: Yellow fever and malaria had badly depleted the French workforce. The Americans put William Gorgas in charge of health. Knowing mosquitoes carried both diseases, his teams drained swamps and standing water, oiled water to kill larvae, and screened hospital wards. The last canal worker to die of yellow fever caught it late in 1906, and the canal opened in August 1914.

title: Lighthouses
objective: After this level you can explain how lighthouses guided ships.
summary: Smeaton's 1759 Eddystone tower, oak-shaped and dovetailed, outlasted its rock. Fresnel's 1822 lens focused light into a beam, and each light signs itself by flash pattern and daymark.

cards.headline: The first Eddystone lighthouse was swept away, and its builder with it.
cards.body: Henry Winstanley finished it in 1698: the first lighthouse built on a small rock in the open sea. A storm in 1703 destroyed it and killed him. The next tower, John Rudyerd's, stood for 47 years until it burned in 1755. How do you build a tower the sea can't beat?

cards.headline: Built like an oak
cards.body: John Smeaton's answer, finished in 1759, was Cornish granite, modeled on the shape of an oak tree for strength. He locked the stones together with dovetailed joints, and used a quick-setting cement that could stand up to salty seawater. It worked: his tower was replaced in 1882 only because the rock beneath it cracked. Its upper part now stands on Plymouth Hoe. The tower outlasted its own foundation.

cards.headline: A lens that catches stray light
cards.body: A lamp shines in every direction, so most of its light never reaches a ship. In 1822 Augustin Fresnel completed a lens design that focuses rays that would normally scatter into a single, intense beam. Large first-order Fresnel lenses shine up to 21 miles out to sea. Same lamp, far more reach.

cards.headline: Every lighthouse signs its name
cards.body: Seeing a light isn't enough: a sailor needs to know which one it is. At night, each lighthouse flashes its own pattern, called its characteristic, listed in light lists and on charts. Today's Eddystone light gives two flashes every 10 seconds. By day, lighthouses wear painted daymarks: Cape Hatteras has black and white spiral stripes, Bodie Island bands, and Cape Lookout a checkerboard.

title: Foundations
objective: After this level you can explain why foundations matter, using the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
summary: Foundations hand the load to the ground: shallow ones spread it, piles reach firm soil. Pisa's tower, on a shallow footing in soft ground, leaned by 1178; engineers pulled it back about 45 cm.

cards.headline: The Leaning Tower of Pisa began leaning when it was two floors tall.
cards.body: Work began in 1173 on a bell tower for Pisa's cathedral. By 1178, with construction up to the second floor, it was already tipping. The trouble wasn't in the stonework. It was underneath.

cards.headline: Where the load path ends
cards.body: Level 2's load path ends in the soil, and a foundation's job is to hand the building over to it. Shallow foundations sit near the surface and spread the load over the soil. Where the soil is weak, piles, long slender columns, carry the load down through it to firmer soil or rock. Pisa's tower stands on a footing only three meters deep, in soft ground that settled unevenly beneath it.

cards.headline: Saved by a war
cards.body: Then war between Italian city-states stopped the work for nearly a century. That pause helped prevent an early collapse: it gave the foundation time to stabilize. When work resumed, the engineer Giovanni di Simone made the new stories slightly taller on the short side to correct the tilt. It backfired, and the tower sank further. It was finished in the 14th century, leaning all the way.

cards.fact: Engineers straightened it by about 45 cm, on purpose.
cards.context: In 1990 the tower closed because its foundations were close to failing. Engineers including Imperial College's John Burland removed 38 cubic meters of soil from under its raised side, letting it settle back toward straight. It reopened in 2001, about 45 cm straighter, back where it stood in 1838. In 2008 engineers announced it had stopped moving. They fixed the tower by fixing the ground.

title: Earthquake-Proof Buildings
objective: After this level you can explain how buildings are designed to survive earthquakes.
summary: Falling buildings are an earthquake's real danger. Unreinforced brick collapses even in small quakes; retrofits tie roofs to walls, and base isolators let the ground move beneath a building.

cards.headline: "Earthquakes don't kill people, buildings do."
cards.body: That saying opens FEMA's page on seismic building codes. It turns earthquake safety into an architecture problem: if the building stays up, the people inside can get out. So which buildings fall, and how do engineers keep them standing?

cards.headline: The most dangerous building on the block
cards.body: Unreinforced masonry means brick walls with little or no steel inside. Remember Level 3: brick and stone are brittle and weak when stretched. In an earthquake, unreinforced brick buildings often collapse both inward and outward, and even relatively small quakes can badly damage them. A pile of bricks is only a wall while nothing shakes it.

cards.headline: Tie it together
cards.body: The fix for old brick buildings starts at the top. Retrofits strengthen the connection between the roof and the walls, so walls and roof support each other instead of falling separately, and they brace chimneys. The goal is modest and life-saving: keep the building intact long enough for people to exit safely.

mascot.line: Level 27's pagoda had a similar instinct: don't fight the quake, let things move.

cards.headline: Or let the ground move without you
cards.body: Between 2004 and 2008, the Utah State Capitol was fitted with 265 base isolators: layers of rubber and steel around a lead core, set between the building and the ground. In a quake the ground can shift the Capitol up to two feet sideways while the building stays relatively still, and the heated lead turns putty-like, soaking up energy. The seismic impact drops by roughly 75 to 80 percent.

title: Checkpoint: Engineering Marvels
objective: After this level you can explain how engineers span rivers, dig tunnels and hold back water.
summary: Galloping Gertie twisted apart in the wind in 1940 because its designers hadn't given that force a path. Every marvel in this chapter finds each force and gives it a way to the ground.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: four months after it opened, a bridge twisted itself apart.
cards.body: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State, nicknamed Galloping Gertie, opened on July 1, 1940. On November 7, 1940, in a wind of about 42 mph, it tore apart. No people died, because the bridge had been closed to traffic in time. What went wrong?

mascot.line: Every marvel in this chapter is a list of forces, each with a path. Gertie's list was missing one.

cards.headline: The force nobody gave a path
cards.body: Its deck was narrow, just two lanes, and stiffened by solid plate girders instead of open trusses. Those girders didn't absorb the wind's gusts, and the deck began to twist, each swing larger than the last. The replacement, opened in 1950, used a web truss, and the collapse spurred research into how wind acts on bridges. Later suspension bridges were designed with its lessons.

title: The First Skyscrapers
objective: After this level you can explain how Chicago built the first skyscrapers.
summary: After the 1871 fire, Chicago's Chicago school built the first skyscrapers, 10 to 15 years later. Sullivan (1896): form ever follows function; the Wainwright Building reads like a column.

cards.headline: In 1871, Chicago burned. Within a generation, it was growing up.
cards.body: The Great Chicago Fire began on October 8, 1871. About 300 people died, and roughly one in three Chicagoans lost their home. The city that rose afterward became famous for a brand-new kind of building. But the fire didn't build it. What did?

cards.headline: Not overnight
cards.body: Right after the fire, Chicago rebuilt fast, and the new buildings looked much like the old ones. What changed quickly was the ground itself: within months, a land rush began. The earliest skyscrapers came 10 to 15 years later, 8 to 10 stories tall, with steel frames, elevators and new kinds of foundations. The fire cleared the ground. It took new ideas to build up from it.

cards.headline: The Chicago school
cards.body: Those ideas came from a group of architects and engineers now called the Chicago school: William Le Baron Jenney, Daniel Burnham, John Root, Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan. Together they developed the skyscraper. Jenney designed the Home Insurance Building (1884–85), generally considered the first tall building held up by an iron and steel skeleton: Level 8's frame, taken up high. Chicago has been called the birthplace of modern architecture.

mascot.line: If you remember one line from this level, make it Sullivan's: form ever follows function.

cards.headline: Form ever follows function
cards.body: A frame could stand tall. But what should a tall building look like? In an 1896 essay, Louis Sullivan answered: "form ever follows function." Give the street floor a grand entrance and big openings for shops. Above it, stack the offices, and since every office is alike, make every window alike, "because they are all alike." Then top it with an attic that shows the offices have ended. The outside tells you what's inside.

cards.fact: The Wainwright Building reads like a classical column.
cards.context: Critics of the day compared a tall building to a column: base, shaft and capital. Adler and Sullivan's 10-story Wainwright Building in St. Louis (1890–91) fits: a two-story stone base, seven stories of unbroken brick piers, and a leafy frieze under an overhanging roof. Sullivan stressed the upright lines and played down the horizontal ones, so your eye runs straight up.

title: Why Elevators Mattered
objective: After this level you can explain how safe elevators made tall buildings possible.
summary: Otis's 1854 safety brake and the 1857 passenger elevator made buildings over four or five stories practical, and turned the attic of the poor into the prized penthouse.

cards.headline: A few seconds in 1854 decided which floor would be the best one.
cards.body: At New York's Crystal Palace, Elisha Otis rode his raised elevator platform in front of a crowd and had its rope cut. The platform held. That little stunt ended up changing what buildings looked like, and who lived at the top.

cards.headline: A brake the rope switches on
cards.body: Otis's safety device gripped the guide rails the moment the hoist rope lost its tension, so a snapped rope set the brake all by itself. In 1857 the first safe passenger elevator went into the E.V. Haughwout store in New York City. It made buildings of more than four or five stories practical. Before that, the limit on a building's height was your legs.

mascot.line: Same top floor, same view. The only thing that changed was the ride up.

cards.headline: The top floor gets promoted
cards.body: Before elevators, the attic was an awkward climb, the retreat of the poor. New York's Equitable Life Assurance Building, finished in 1870, is said to be the city's first office building with a passenger elevator, and it made its upper floors as convenient as the lower ones, and even more desirable. By the 1920s the old attic had become the sought-after penthouse.

cards.fact: The elevator helped draw the modern city.
cards.context: By opening the way to higher buildings, the elevator played a decisive role in creating the urban geography of many modern cities. Remember Level 61's first skyscrapers, with steel frames and elevators? The frame let a building stand tall. The elevator made its upper floors worth having.

title: The Empire State Building
objective: After this level you can explain how it went up in about a year.
summary: The 102-story Empire State Building went up in about 410 days (1930-31), its frame rising 4.5 stories a week, thanks to overlapping design and building and just-in-time deliveries.

cards.headline: The Empire State Building took about 410 days.
cards.body: Work began on March 17, 1930. On May 1, 1931, President Herbert Hoover pressed a button in Washington, D.C., to open it. That's a 102-story skyscraper in a little over a year. How do you build that fast?

cards.headline: Four and a half stories a week
cards.body: The steel framework rose at about four and a half stories per week. Picture it: in the time it takes you to get through one week of school, the tower grew four floors, with half a floor to spare. The architects were Shreve, Lamb & Harmon, and the builders were Starrett Bros. & Eken.

cards.headline: Building before the drawings were done
cards.body: The speed came from planning, not magic. Construction began before the design was finished, so builders worked while Level 9's drawings were still being made. Foundations were dug while the old Waldorf-Astoria hotel on the site was still being torn down. Deliveries arrived just in time, so little had to be stored, and railway tracks on site moved materials around. Here's an analogy: an assembly line where the factory grows upward.

cards.fact: It was the world's tallest building until 1970.
cards.context: It's one of the best examples of Art Deco design, and it rose 1,250 feet (381 meters) with its spire. That spire had an ambitious first job: it was meant to be a mooring station for airships.

title: Wind and Tall Buildings
objective: After this level you can explain how tall buildings resist the wind.
summary: Vortices shed from alternate sides push a tower across the wind and, in time with its sway, rock it harder. Changing shape confuses the wind; dampers like Taipei 101's steady it.

cards.headline: Near the top of Taipei 101 hangs a steel ball weighing 660 metric tons.
cards.body: It's suspended between the 87th and 92nd floors, in the middle of the building, and its job is to keep the tower steady in strong winds. Why would a skyscraper need to hang a giant ball inside itself? Because wind does something sneaky to tall buildings.

mascot.line: Hold on to this sideways tug; the next level's tower is shaped to beat it.

cards.headline: Pushed across the wind
cards.body: Level 2 called wind a sideways live load. Here's the sneaky part. As wind flows past a tall building, swirls of air called vortices form and break away, first from one side, then the other. Each one tugs the building. So it gets pushed and pulled across the wind's direction, not just along it.

cards.headline: Pushing the swing
cards.body: Think of pushing a child on a swing: time your pushes to the swing's natural rhythm and it goes higher and higher. If the vortices break away in time with a building's own natural sway, they rock it harder the same way. At a minimum, life on the upper floors gets uncomfortable.

cards.headline: Confuse the wind
cards.body: So engineers break the rhythm. Change a tower's shape as it rises and the vortices lose their coherence: the wind, in engineers' words, becomes confused. Softened corners and openings for the wind to blow through help too, and designs are tested in wind tunnels. When shape isn't enough, a damper like Taipei 101's steel ball steadies the sway.

title: The Burj Khalifa
objective: After this level you can describe the world's tallest building.
summary: Burj Khalifa (2010, 828 m, CTBUH tallest as of 2026), by SOM's Adrian Smith and William F. Baker: a Y plan from a desert flower, a buttressed core, and spiral setbacks that confuse the wind.

cards.headline: The world's tallest building takes its shape from a desert flower.
cards.body: As of 2026, the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH) ranks Dubai's Burj Khalifa, completed in 2010, as the tallest building in the world: 828 meters. Its shape isn't just decoration. It's how the tower stands up to the wind.

cards.headline: A flower in plan
cards.body: The firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) designed it, with Adrian Smith as architect and William F. Baker as structural engineer, and it formally opened on January 4, 2010. Look down on it and you see a Y: three wings around a center, an abstract version of the local Hymenocallis flower, drawing on patterns of Islamic architecture. The Y also points views out toward the Arabian Gulf.

cards.headline: A core with three buttresses
cards.body: At the middle stands a six-sided concrete core. Each wing has its own concrete core and perimeter columns, and the three wings brace the center from three sides: a buttressed core. Here's an analogy: a camera tripod, whose spread legs keep the top from tipping whichever way it's nudged.

cards.headline: Confusing the wind, at full height
cards.body: Remember Level 64's trick? As the tower rises, its wings step back in a spiral. So the wind meets a different building shape at each tier, and its vortices can never gather into a rhythm. SOM calls it confusing the wind, and wind-tunnel tests backed the plan. The Y shape itself also cuts the wind forces on the tower.

title: Glass Towers
objective: After this level you can explain the curtain walls of glass towers.
summary: A curtain wall is a nonbearing skin hung on the frame. Air conditioning and cheap postwar energy made glass towers practical; Lever House (1952) led in New York. Glass's catch: solar heat.

cards.headline: In 2013, a London skyscraper melted parts of a car.
cards.body: Sunlight bounced off the curved glass face of 20 Fenchurch Street, nicknamed the Walkie-Talkie, and was concentrated onto the street below, where it melted part of a parked Jaguar. So how did so many towers end up wrapped in glass?

cards.headline: A wall that hangs
cards.body: Level 8 split the jobs: the frame carries the floors, and the outer wall holds up only itself, hanging on the frame. That outer skin is called a curtain wall: a nonbearing wall of glass, metal or masonry attached to the building's structural frame. The name fits. Like a curtain, it hangs from something else and holds nothing up.

cards.headline: Glass needed cheap energy
cards.body: All-glass towers only became practical in the mid-20th century, with better air conditioning and cheap, plentiful energy. After World War II, low energy costs boosted the idea of the tower as a glass prism. In New York, Lever House (1952), designed by Gordon Bunshaft of SOM, was the first commercial building with a glass curtain wall, its glass held by extruded aluminum. It was widely copied.

cards.fact: Glass buildings have always had a heat problem.
cards.context: Even Level 8's Crystal Palace suffered: records show its indoor temperatures were extremely unstable, and it amplified peak summer heat. Glass lets the sun in, and a curved glass face can concentrate it too. After the Walkie-Talkie's glare, a permanent sunshade of horizontal aluminum fins was approved for the tower.

title: Building a Skyscraper
objective: After this level you can describe the steps from foundation to top.
summary: A skyscraper starts with a pit and piles to bedrock; a concrete core climbs first, the steel frame follows, floors go on steel decking, and the outer wall and fit-out overlap.

cards.headline: A skyscraper starts by going down.
cards.body: Before anything rises, builders dig a pit to hold the foundation. Then the tower grows in layers, and several of those layers are being built at the same time. Here's the order, from the bottom up.

cards.headline: Down to rock
cards.body: Piles, which are vertical beams, are sunk through the soil until they're embedded in the bedrock. That's where Level 2's load path ends. A continuous path carries the loads from the roof down through the building to the foundation, and into the ground that holds it all up. For a piled tower, that ground is rock.

cards.headline: The core goes first
cards.body: Many towers are built core-first. A concrete core, holding the stairways, elevators and utility risers, is cast inside a self-climbing form: a giant mold that climbs as the core rises. The steel framing follows once the forms have climbed clear. Here's an analogy: the spine grows first, and the rest of the skeleton catches up.

cards.headline: Frame, floor, skin
cards.body: Cranes lift each steel beam into place, where skilled workers bolt or weld it. Thin corrugated steel decking goes down on the beams, and about 5 to 10 cm of concrete is poured on top to make a floor. Panels of glass, metal or stone are bolted to the frame as the outer wall, then come wiring, pipes and elevators. All of it overlaps: frame at the top, walls and wiring lower down.

title: Safety on Site
objective: After this level you can explain how construction workers are kept safe.
summary: The 1932 'Lunch atop a Skyscraper' photo shows the old risks. Falls are construction's leading killer; US fall protection starts at six feet. Hard hats began as miners' canvas helmets.

cards.headline: Eleven men ate lunch on a steel beam, 850 feet above New York.
cards.body: The photo was taken on September 20, 1932, high on the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center. It's one of the most famous pictures of building work ever made. Today it's also a lesson in exactly what not to do.

cards.headline: Staged, but real
cards.body: The men were real ironworkers, used to walking the girders of the very building they were putting up. The scene was posed: they were humoring a photographer who was drumming up excitement about the project. So the danger in the picture wasn't invented. It was their everyday workplace, with a camera added.

cards.fact: Falls are the leading cause of death in construction.
cards.context: That's from the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). In 2024 there were 389 fatal falls to a lower level out of 1,034 construction deaths: more than a third. So US rules require fall protection in construction from six feet up, about the height of a tall person. It comes in layers: guardrails and toe-boards around open edges, safety harnesses and lines, and safety nets.

cards.headline: The hat came from a mine
cards.body: After World War I, Edward W. Bullard made a helmet for miners at risk from falling debris, inspired by the steel "doughboy" helmets soldiers had worn. It was heavy canvas steamed into shape with glue, so he called it the Hard Boiled Hat. The idea spread to big building jobs, and Hoover Dam became the first project where employers required hard hats.

title: The Race to the Top
objective: After this level you can explain the race to build the tallest building.
summary: The Chrysler Building won 1929's race with a secret spire; the CTBUH counts spires, not antennas, which let the Petronas Towers pass the Sears Tower in 1998. The title moved from New York to Dubai.

cards.headline: On October 23, 1929, a secret spire rose out of the Chrysler Building.
cards.body: It had been assembled inside the building's crown in five sections. Then it was hoisted into place in about 90 minutes. The Chrysler Building was racing another tower for the title of the world's tallest, and this was the winning move.

cards.headline: The rival downtown
cards.body: The rival was 40 Wall Street, rising at the same time downtown. The Chrysler's architect, William Van Alen, kept his trump card hidden until the last moment, and the finished tower stood 1,046 feet tall. The victory didn't last. Built between 1928 and 1930, it held the record only until the Empire State Building opened in 1931.

mascot.line: Moral of the story: if you're racing, wear a pointy hat, not an antenna.

cards.headline: What counts as the top?
cards.body: A race needs rules. In 1998 the Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur took the title from Chicago's Sears Tower, even though the Sears roof was more than 200 feet higher. The Petronas spires were counted as part of the architecture. Today the CTBUH measures to a building's architectural top: spires count, antennas don't.

title: Checkpoint: Skyscrapers
objective: After this level you can explain what makes skyscrapers possible and how they stay up.
summary: 'Skyscraper' was a sail before it was a building (1888, Chicago). New York's 1916 zoning, after the Equitable's shadow, shaped wedding-cake towers. Frames, elevators and wind strategies do the rest.

cards.headline: Skyscrapers recap: before it was a building, a skyscraper was a sail.
cards.body: In 1794, a skyscraper was a light sail at the very top of a ship's mast. Here's how the word climbed onto buildings, and how one city's law gave its skyline a shape.

cards.headline: A word for tall things
cards.body: The word was used for all sorts of high-reaching things, even a racehorse, before it was first recorded for a very tall city building in 1888, in a Chicago context. That's the Chicago of Level 61's Chicago school. Other languages chose the same picture: German says Wolkenkratzer, "cloud scraper," and French says gratte-ciel, "scrape-sky."

mascot.line: Next time you see a stepped New York tower, you're looking at a law, drawn in stone.

cards.headline: The law that stepped the skyline
cards.body: In 1915, New York's Equitable Building rose straight up, with no setbacks, to 538 feet, and cast a seven-acre shadow over its neighbors. The city answered with its 1916 Zoning Resolution, the nation's first comprehensive zoning ordinance, which controlled the size and shape of buildings. It fostered slender towers and tiered "wedding cake" buildings. Those steps began with a shadow, not with the wind.

title: Gaudí
objective: After this level you can describe Gaudí's curving buildings and mosaics in Barcelona.
summary: Gaudí designed the Sagrada Família with upside-down hanging models and columns that lean like trees, and covered curves in trencadís, a mosaic of broken tile.

cards.headline: Gaudí took over a Barcelona church in 1883. Its central tower rose in 2026.
cards.body: The church is the Sagrada Família. It occupied Antoni Gaudí until he died in 1926, when only one transept, with one of its towers, was finished. Builders completed its central Tower of Jesus Christ in February 2026, and finishing work goes on. How do you design a building that outlives you by a century? Gaudí started with string.

mascot.line: Gravity did the sums. Gaudí just had to hold the drawing upside down.

cards.headline: Design it upside down
cards.body: Remember Level 10's hanging chain? Gaudí turned it into a design tool. He hung networks of cords and loaded them with small bags of weight, standing in for the stone each arch would carry. A hanging cord is in pure tension. Turn its shape upside down and the forces become compression, running along the curve. He worked the method out for a church at the Colònia Güell, near Barcelona, then carried it into the Sagrada Família.

cards.headline: Columns that lean like trees
cards.body: Level 4's arches push outward at their feet, a diagonal thrust that massive supports must resist. Gaudí wanted his buildings to stand without buttresses propping them from outside, the way a tree stands. So his piers and columns tilt, leaning along the diagonal thrust they carry. Inside the Sagrada Família they rise like a forest of twisting stone trunks. The lean isn't a wobble. It's the force, made visible.

cards.fact: Gaudí covered his curves in broken tile.
cards.context: The technique is called trencadís: a mosaic of broken ceramic pieces. Small pieces can follow a curved surface that flat, whole tiles can't. Its best-known showcase is the long, undulating bench in Park Güell, glittering with color. UNESCO lists seven of Gaudí's works in and near Barcelona as World Heritage, first inscribed in 1984 and extended in 2005.

title: Frank Lloyd Wright
objective: After this level you can explain Fallingwater and buildings that fit their landscape.
summary: Wright set Fallingwater over a waterfall on concrete cantilevers echoing the rock ledges. Cantilevers are stretched on top, and the terraces sagged until steel cables fixed them.

cards.headline: A family wanted to look at their waterfall. Wright built their house over it.
cards.body: The Kaufmanns loved the falls on Bear Run, in Pennsylvania, and expected a house facing them, where they could admire the water from afar. Frank Lloyd Wright cantilevered the house directly over the falls instead. He designed it in 1935 as the family's weekend retreat, and it was finished in 1937. It's called Fallingwater.

cards.headline: A house that belongs to its rocks
cards.body: Wright called his approach organic architecture: a building in harmony with its site, joining people and nature. At Fallingwater he echoed the rock ledges along the stream. The house is a stack of concrete trays, each anchored to a central chimney built of local sandstone. Outside, the ledges are stone. The ones you stand on are concrete. From the living room, the stream isn't a view. It's underneath you.

mascot.line: People mix these two up: a cantilever bends the opposite way from Level 3's lintel.

cards.headline: The cantilever: a beam held at one end
cards.body: A cantilever is a beam supported at only one end, with the other end free. (A diving board is one.) It bends the opposite way from Level 3's lintel. A lintel is stretched along its underside; a loaded cantilever is stretched along its upper half and squeezed along its lower half. Concrete handles stretching badly, so Fallingwater's concrete terraces carry steel reinforcing rods inside.

cards.fact: Fallingwater's terraces sagged.
cards.context: By 1955 the Kaufmanns had measured them tilting down about four inches. Decades later, in 2001 and 2002, engineers anchored bundles of high-strength steel cable into the concrete below the house, ran them along the big beams under the living room and tightened them. The sagging stopped. Level 7's lesson, applied late: when concrete is stretched, steel has to take the tension.

title: Le Corbusier
objective: After this level you can explain the idea of a house as a machine for living in.
summary: Le Corbusier called a house a machine for living in. His Dom-ino frame freed walls, leading to five points: pilotis, roof garden, free plan, long windows, free facade, shown in the Villa Savoye.

cards.headline: In 1923, Le Corbusier wrote that a house is a machine for living in.
cards.body: The line comes from his book Vers une architecture: "La maison est une machine à habiter." It sounds cold. He meant that a house should first serve the body, giving comfort as efficiently as a good machine. Only then, he said, does it become a place for meditation and for beauty. So what does a living machine look like?

cards.headline: Dom-ino: a house as a kit
cards.body: In 1914 he drew the Dom-ino system: three concrete floor slabs, six posts and a staircase. That's the whole thing. As in Level 8's frame, the skeleton carries the floors, so no wall has to hold anything up. Walls can go anywhere, windows can run the full length of the front, and the module can be repeated again and again. The rest of his career grew out of this kit.

cards.headline: Five points, and a garage built to fit the car
cards.body: In 1927 he set out five points for a new architecture: pilotis (posts that lift the house off the ground), a roof garden, a free plan, long horizontal windows and a free facade. Every one follows from the frame. The Villa Savoye at Poissy, France, built from 1928 to 1931, shows them best. Its ground floor even curves to match the turning radius of the family car, which drove in under the pilotis. A machine for living, with the car's needs designed right in.

cards.fact: Seventeen of Le Corbusier's works are World Heritage.
cards.context: UNESCO listed them together in 2016, spread across seven countries. Seven countries, one architect, one listing.

title: The Bauhaus
objective: After this level you can explain Bauhaus design.
summary: Gropius's Bauhaus (1919-33) taught art and craft together, aimed design at factories, gave us Breuer's bicycle-inspired steel chair and built a Dessau home whose fittings came from its own workshops.

cards.headline: At the Bauhaus, every workshop had two teachers: an artist and a craftsman.
cards.body: Walter Gropius founded the school in Weimar, Germany, in 1919, by combining an academy of arts with a school of arts and crafts. Two teachers per workshop was the whole idea in miniature.

cards.headline: Art, meet the factory
cards.body: The Bauhaus set out to end the split between art and craft by training students equally in both. In each workshop, an artist called the Form Master taught theory while a craftsman taught technique. Then Gropius pointed the work at mass manufacture rather than one-off handmade pieces. The goal wasn't a single beautiful chair. It was a beautiful chair a factory could make thousands of.

cards.fact: A famous Bauhaus chair began with a bicycle.
cards.context: Marcel Breuer designed his tubular steel club chair in 1925, the year he became master of the school's cabinet-making workshop. The curved handlebars of his bicycle had shown him that bent steel tube was light, strong and suited to industrial production, just what the Bauhaus wanted. Today the chair is often called the Wassily chair.

cards.headline: A school that furnished itself
cards.body: In 1925 the Bauhaus moved to Dessau, and Gropius's office designed its new building, which opened in December 1926. Its workshop wing wears a steel and glass facade drawn around it like a curtain, so you can see into the workshops from outside. Inside, the lamps and tubular steel furniture came from the school's own workshops; Gropius designed the door handles. The school moved to Berlin in 1932, and the Nazi regime forced it to close in 1933.

title: Less Is More
objective: After this level you can explain Mies van der Rohe's minimalism.
summary: Mies's motto was less is more. In his Barcelona Pavilion, thin steel columns hold the roof so stone and glass walls stand freely; his glass Farnsworth House met a river that ignored the plans.

cards.headline: Mies's Barcelona Pavilion was taken apart in 1930. Then it came back.
cards.body: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich designed it as Germany's pavilion for the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition. After the fair, it was dismantled. From 1983 to 1986 it was rebuilt on its original site. Why rebuild a building that was so small and held so little?

cards.headline: Less is more
cards.body: That was Mies's motto: less is more, an architecture of elegant simplicity. (He later ran the Bauhaus, from 1930 until the Nazi regime forced it to close in 1933.) In the pavilion, eight slender chrome-clad steel columns hold up a flat roof. That frees the walls, of glass, travertine, green marble and golden onyx, to stand wherever he wanted, like screens you wander between. Few parts, rich materials, nothing extra: the fewest, finest pieces doing all the talking.

cards.headline: A glass box on a floodplain
cards.body: The Farnsworth House near Chicago, designed in 1945 and built in 1950-51, is less at its purest: a glass box raised on steel on the floodplain of the Fox River. With glass on every side, the outdoors becomes the decoration. Mies set its floor one foot above the highest flood recorded at the time. The river didn't read the plans. In the 1996 flood, water stood more than five feet deep inside.

title: The Sydney Opera House
objective: After this level you can describe its sail-like roofs and how they were built.
summary: Utzon's winning shells took years to make buildable, until every shell was cut from one sphere, so the roof could be made of standard parts. Utzon resigned in 1966; the building opened in 1973.

cards.headline: In 1957, Jørn Utzon won a competition with a roof nobody knew how to build.
cards.body: The Danish architect's design beat 233 entries in the international competition for a Sydney opera house. It showed a cluster of sail-like shells rising over the harbor. Beautiful, and for years, impossible.

mascot.line: When every curve is different, nothing repeats. Make them all one curve, and suddenly you have a kit.

cards.headline: Every shell, cut from one sphere
cards.body: To build a shell, the engineers at Arup needed its shape as mathematics. From 1958 to 1962, Utzon's team tried parabolas, then ellipses, and neither worked. By late 1961 Utzon saw the key: every shell could be cut from the surface of a single sphere. One shared curve meant the roof could be split into standard parts, prefabricated and assembled on site. Picture every piece of a peel coming from the same ball.

cards.fact: The famous orange story is a myth.
cards.context: Popular legend says Utzon peeled an orange and saw the roof. The Sydney Opera House itself calls that a popular myth. An orange can show how the geometry works, but the breakthrough was Utzon noticing that the shells were so alike that one form, a sphere, could produce them all.

cards.headline: The architect who never came back
cards.body: The shells were solved; the politics were not. In February 1966, after a dispute with the New South Wales government, Utzon resigned, and a team led by Peter Hall took over the design. Utzon left Australia that April and never returned to see his building finished. It was completed in 1973 and joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2007.

title: Zaha Hadid
objective: After this level you can describe Hadid's flowing buildings.
summary: Long called a paper architect, Zaha Hadid designed through painting, built the angular Vitra Fire Station in 1993, and later folded whole plazas into buildings. In 2004 she won the Pritzker Prize.

cards.headline: For years, Zaha Hadid was labeled a paper architect.
cards.body: She kept winning competitions, starting with The Peak, a leisure club in Hong Kong, in 1983. But her winning designs often went unbuilt. In 2004 she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize. How do you get from paper to that?

cards.headline: Designing with paint
cards.body: Hadid was born in Baghdad in 1950, studied mathematics in Beirut, then trained as an architect in London. Especially early on, painting and drawing were how she investigated a design. Her work drew on Kazimir Malevich and the Suprematist painters, and it shared their sense of fragmentation, instability and movement. Her paintings weren't illustrations of buildings. They were how she found them.

cards.fact: Her first major building was a fire station.
cards.context: The Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, Germany, was finished in 1993: a series of sharply angled, tilted planes of exposed concrete. Her office called it "movement frozen", a building tense and alert, ready to explode into action when the alarm rang. It no longer houses fire engines; it's used for exhibitions and events.

cards.headline: From shards to waves
cards.body: Her later buildings flow. Her office's Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, completed in 2012, seems to rise out of its plaza as if the ground itself had been lifted, curved and folded. Floor, wall, ceiling and roof blur into one surface. The sharp shards of the fire station had become long, continuous waves.

title: Brutalism
objective: After this level you can explain raw concrete buildings and why people argue about them.
summary: Brutalism comes from béton brut, raw concrete, not from brutal. Banham praised buildings made of what they appear to be made of; fans see post-war ambition, critics a dystopia.

cards.headline: One building: 'elephant droppings' to a prince, Stonehenge to a writer.
cards.body: Portsmouth's Tricorn Centre opened in 1966, and the critic Ian Nairn cheered: "At last there is something to shout about in Portsmouth." Prince Charles later called it "a mildewed lump of elephant droppings"; the writer Jonathan Meades compared it to Stonehenge. It was demolished in 2004. Welcome to Brutalism.

mascot.line: People hear 'brutal'. The name most likely comes from béton brut: raw concrete.

cards.headline: Not brutal: raw
cards.body: The name doesn't come from brutal. It probably comes from béton brut, French for raw concrete, Le Corbusier's phrase while building his Unité d'Habitation in 1952. Yes, Level 73's machine-for-living man. From the 1950s he left his materials unfinished, including concrete still printed with the marks of the formwork it was cast in. You can read how a wall was made just by looking at it.

cards.headline: Made of what it appears to be made of
cards.body: In a 1955 essay, the critic Reyner Banham named a trend in British architecture "The New Brutalism". His model was a school at Hunstanton by Alison and Peter Smithson: a building "made of what it appears to be made of". No decoration, nothing hidden. And it wasn't only concrete. The Smithsons wanted every material, brick, timber or glass, honestly expressed.

cards.headline: Loved and loathed
cards.body: Historic England calls Brutalism loved and loathed, one of the most controversial styles of the 20th century. To its fans, it shows the post-war drive to rebuild towns so they served people better. To its critics, it was a dystopian landscape-destroyer. The Tricorn's fans and foes were looking at the same raw concrete and seeing opposite things.

title: The Guggenheim Bilbao
objective: After this level you can explain how one museum changed a city.
summary: Gehry's 1997 museum used aerospace software and titanium skin. Its crowds gave rise to the 'Bilbao effect', which critic Witold Rybczynski argued rarely repeats.

cards.headline: Can one building turn a city around? Bilbao bet a museum on it.
cards.body: The city of Bilbao grew on iron, steel and shipbuilding, and it went through a severe economic crisis in the 1970s and 1980s. In 1997 it opened a new art museum designed by Frank Gehry, a joint venture of the Guggenheim Foundation and the Basque regional government.

cards.headline: Designed with aerospace software
cards.body: Gehry's curves were mathematically complex, so his team used CATIA, software first built for the aerospace industry, to turn his design into a structure and help the builders. Then the skin. Gehry chose titanium after watching how a sample pinned up outside his office behaved. About 33,000 thin titanium sheets now cover the museum, and they change color with the weather and the light.

cards.headline: The Bilbao effect
cards.body: The museum drew about 20 million visitors in its first 20 years, and the former industrial city became a major tourist destination. People began to talk of a Bilbao effect: the idea that one iconic building can transform a city's fortunes.

cards.headline: The skeptic
cards.body: The critic Witold Rybczynski wasn't convinced. In 2011 he argued that nobody had checked whether eye-catching museum architecture really brings the crowds, and that it doesn't, pointing to museums in Seattle and Denver. His title for it: the Bilbao anomaly. One spectacular success, in other words, doesn't make a rule.

title: Checkpoint: Modern Masters

summary: The Pritzker Prize (1979) honors a living architect's built work. Modern masters found form in nature, in the machine and in new geometry.

cards.headline: Modern Masters finale: architecture has its own Nobel. Three of ours won it.
cards.body: Frank Gehry won the Pritzker Prize in 1989, Jørn Utzon in 2003 and Zaha Hadid in 2004, the first woman to win. What does the prize reward? And how do this chapter's ideas fit together?

cards.headline: The Pritzker Prize
cards.body: The Pritzker family of Chicago set up the prize in 1979, through their Hyatt Foundation. Each year it honors a living architect whose built work shows talent, vision and commitment. It's often called architecture's Nobel, and many of its procedures are modeled on the Nobel Prize. The winner receives $100,000 and a bronze medallion. Note the word built: Hadid, the former paper architect, won for buildings that stood.

title: The First Cities
objective: After this level you can describe early cities like Uruk.
summary: Childe listed signs of the first cities: size, big public works, writing, full-time specialists. By about 3200 BCE Uruk had them all, and its first writing was bookkeeping.

cards.headline: Around 3200 BCE, the biggest settlement on Earth may have been in Iraq.
cards.body: It was Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, in what is now southeastern Iraq. But a big crowd of houses isn't automatically a city. So what turns a settlement into one? Archaeologists have a checklist, and Uruk ticks the boxes.

cards.headline: A checklist for a city
cards.body: The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe listed 10 signs of the earliest cities. Among them: a bigger settlement than any village, large-scale public works, writing, and full-time specialists, people who do one job all day instead of farming. Think of it as a city's ID card. A village has houses. A city has houses plus a temple crew, a scribe and a wall builder.

cards.headline: Mud brick, dressed up
cards.body: Uruk's public works were monumental buildings of mud brick. Their walls were covered in mosaics made from painted clay cones, pressed in like pushpins in a corkboard. Around the whole city ran brick walls about 10 km long. Legend says the hero Gilgamesh built them. Whoever did, it took a great many bricks.

cards.fact: The first writing was bookkeeping.
cards.context: The earliest written records in Sumerian are picture-sign tablets from Uruk, from about the end of the 4th millennium BCE. They aren't poems or prayers. They're lists and ledgers of goods, with numbers and names. A city full of specialists has to keep track of who handed over what. The first writers were, in effect, accountants.

title: Grid Cities
objective: After this level you can explain grid street plans from ancient cities to New York.
summary: Grids are ancient (Mohenjo-daro), named for Hippodamus and used by Roman towns and Penn's Philadelphia. New York's 1811 grid was chosen because right-angled houses are cheapest.

cards.headline: In 1811, New York drew a grid over Manhattan, all the way to 155th Street.
cards.body: Look at a map of Manhattan today and you're looking at that decision. The commissioners who drew it later explained why, in one refreshingly blunt sentence. But first: they didn't invent the grid. Not even close.

cards.headline: Older than the Greeks
cards.body: Mohenjo-daro, the largest city of the Indus civilization (about 2600 to 1900 BCE), was laid out with remarkable regularity in about a dozen blocks. Much later, the Greek planner Hippodamus of Miletus, who laid out Athens's port of Piraeus, gave his name to grid plans. He didn't invent them; he just got the credit, like a band covering a song so well that people forget the original.

cards.headline: Easy to measure, easy to divide
cards.body: Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles. In 1682, William Penn gave Philadelphia a grid, and the idea traveled west with American pioneers for a practical reason: it was the simplest way to divide surveyed land. A grid turns a wild landscape into lots you can number, measure and hand out.

cards.fact: New York chose squares because squares are cheap.
cards.context: The 1811 commissioners wrote that straight-sided, right-angled houses "are the most cheap to build, and the most convenient to live in." No grand theory, no symbolism: a city is mostly homes, and boxy homes are the thriftiest. Manhattan's grid is a cost estimate you can walk around in.

title: Walls and Gates
objective: After this level you can explain why cities built walls and what happened when they came down.
summary: Walls gave towns security, paid for by taxes like murage, with gates for carts and walkers. As cities grew, walls cramped them; many came down and became boulevards, like Vienna's Ringstrasse.

cards.headline: The word boulevard once meant the top of a city wall.
cards.body: It comes from French for the flat top of a rampart, a garbled borrowing of Middle Dutch bolwerc, the same word that gave English bulwark. So how does a wall turn into a wide, leafy street?

cards.headline: Security you paid for
cards.body: Fears of invasion, uprising and civil war made medieval town walls seem a necessary security. They weren't cheap: English towns could get royal permission to collect a tax called murage to pay for work on their walls. Carts and people came and went through the gates. A main gate could have several archways: a big one for carts and wagons, and one or two smaller ones for people on foot.

cards.headline: The wall becomes the problem
cards.body: But a wall doesn't grow when the town does. As cities filled up, walls caused overcrowding, blocked out air and light, and led to very poor sanitation. By the 18th century, walls and gates looked like an obstacle to growth and traffic, and gates were often pulled down as too narrow. It's a belt the town has outgrown, and nobody can loosen it.

mascot.line: Next time you see a ring road hugging an old town, look for the wall it replaced.

cards.headline: Wall down, boulevard up
cards.body: In the late 17th century, Louis XIV had an old Paris wall razed and replaced with a wide tree-lined promenade: a boulevard, for strolling along the line of the old wall. Vienna did it on a grand scale. On 20 December 1857, Emperor Franz Joseph ordered the city walls torn down for the Ringstrasse, a ring-shaped boulevard whose first section opened in 1865. The ring road is the ghost of the ring wall.

title: Parks
objective: After this level you can explain why cities build parks.
summary: Paxton's Birkenhead Park (1847), paid for by houses around it, inspired Olmsted. His Central Park, with Vaux (1858), is a hand-built landscape for a crowded city, with crosstown roads hidden below.

cards.headline: The man who sketched the Crystal Palace also built a park that changed cities.
cards.body: Remember Level 8's Joseph Paxton, doodling the Crystal Palace on blotting paper? He also designed Birkenhead Park, opened in 1847, the first public park in the UK created at public expense. Why would a city pay for grass?

cards.headline: A park that paid for itself
cards.body: Birkenhead didn't just spend money on its park. It made money around it: the park was paid for from the profit on house plots sold around its edge. Houses on the rim paid for the green in the middle. A park that financed itself, which is the kind of gardening accountants enjoy.

cards.headline: The People's Garden
cards.body: In 1850, an American named Frederick Law Olmsted walked through Birkenhead Park. He wrote that democratic America had nothing comparable with this "People's Garden." Eight years later, in 1858, Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux won the competition to design New York's Central Park with their Greensward plan.

cards.headline: Nature, built by hand
cards.body: Central Park was planned as New York's population boomed and many immigrants lived in crowded, unhealthy conditions. It looks wild, but every bit of it is man-made and built by hand; workers planted 500,000 trees, shrubs and vines. Even the traffic is designed: the Greensward plan hid the crosstown roads below the landscape, out of sight. The meadow is as much architecture as any building.

title: Streets and Squares
objective: After this level you can explain how public squares bring people together.
summary: Siena's Campo was built as a meeting place. Whyte found people sit where there's seating; Jacobs argued busy streets are safe streets; Copenhagen's car-free Strøget (1962) thrived.

cards.headline: Siena paved its main square to point at the government.
cards.body: Siena's Piazza del Campo is shaped like a shell, and its brick paving is divided into nine parts that all point toward the Palazzo Pubblico, the seat of government. What makes a public space pull people in?

cards.headline: A square made for meeting
cards.body: The nine parts recall the Government of the Nine, which ruled Siena from 1287 to 1355. But the Campo was made for everyone: a meeting place for citizens, with markets, games and political events. It still hosts the Palio horse race twice a year. A good square is the town's living room, with the town hall as the armchair everyone faces.

cards.headline: Give people somewhere to sit
cards.body: How do you tell a good plaza from a bad one? William H. Whyte simply watched. Filming New York plazas with time-lapse cameras, he found that "people tend to sit where there are places to sit" (1980). It sounds obvious. It took cameras to prove it: sitting space mattered more than open space. A huge empty plaza loses to a small one with good ledges.

cards.headline: Eyes upon the street
cards.body: In The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961), Jane Jacobs argued that a well-used street is apt to be a safe one. Her key ingredient: "eyes upon the street," from shops and homes whose windows face it. A blank wall watches nothing. A row of windows is a neighborhood watch that never signs up.

cards.fact: Copenhagen took the cars off its main street in 1962.
cards.context: Strøget was made car-free as an experiment, despite warnings that no cars would mean no customers. According to the Global Designing Cities Initiative, it succeeded and increased revenue for local shops. The street became what Siena's square always was: a place to be, not just a way through.

title: Subways
objective: After this level you can explain how subways changed cities.
summary: London's Metropolitan Railway (1863) ran steam trains through cut-and-cover trenches; electric deep tubes followed in 1890. The railway then sold 'Metro-land' and built suburbs for its commuters.

cards.headline: In 1863, Londoners rode steam trains under the streets.
cards.body: The world's first underground railway, London's Metropolitan Railway, opened on 10 January 1863, hauled by steam locomotives. Picture a smoky train in a tunnel. How did they build it, and what did it do to the city above?

cards.headline: Dig up the street, then put it back
cards.body: The Metropolitan was built by cut and cover. Workers dug trenches along the streets, gave them brick sides, and roofed them over with iron girders or a brick arch. Then the street went back on top. It's the way you'd bury a garden hose: dig a trench, lay it in, cover it up. Just with a train, and a very inconvenienced London.

cards.headline: Deeper, and electric
cards.body: Cut and cover meant digging up whole streets. In 1890 London opened the first electric underground railway, the first deep "tube," dug by tunnelling instead of trenching. A deep tunnel runs far below the streets instead of in a trench just under them, so the street above can stay put.

mascot.line: Hold on to this: in the next level, suburbs keep following the ride.

cards.fact: A railway that grew its own passengers.
cards.context: In 1915 the Metropolitan Railway began selling the countryside along its line as "Metro-land," a place for commuters to live. From 1919, a company it set up built housing estates on spare land the railway owned. The trains didn't just serve the suburbs; they created them. Build the line, then build the homes that fill the trains.
