title: Suburbs and Sprawl
objective: After this level you can explain how cars shaped suburbs.
summary: Suburbs follow transport: ferries, trains, then cars. Postwar highways (1956) and mass-built towns like Levittown spread them. UN-Habitat and Robert Bruegmann disagree about sprawl.

cards.headline: After World War II, a builder made a whole town like a product line.
cards.body: Levittown, New York, built by Levitt and Sons from 1946 to 1951, was an early completely preplanned, mass-produced housing development: more than 17,000 homes. It became a national symbol of suburbia. How do suburbs like it spread so far from the city? Follow the transport.

cards.headline: Suburbs follow the ride
cards.body: Suburbs have always grown along transport. Brooklyn Heights grew after an 1814 ferry to Manhattan; later came trolley-car suburbs, and in London, Level 86's Metro-land along the railway. Each new ride stretched how far from work people could live. After World War II, federal policy and highway construction sped up the growth of American suburbs.

cards.fact: 41,000 miles of new highway, mostly paid by Washington.
cards.context: The Federal-Aid Highway Act, signed on 29 June 1956, authorized 41,000 miles of interstate highways, with the federal government paying 90 percent. A ferry or a train line runs where it runs; a road network reaches much further. Highways were part of the postwar push that sped up the suburbs.

title: Housing for Everyone
objective: After this level you can explain informal settlements and public housing.
summary: UN-Habitat counts over 1.1 billion people in slums or informal settlements. Vienna's Karl-Marx-Hof and Aravena's 'half of a good house' show two answers: city-built homes and homes families finish.

cards.headline: More than 1.1 billion people live in slums or informal settlements.
cards.body: That's UN-Habitat's count. It's a design problem, but not one about beautiful buildings. It's about whether a home is safe, big enough and truly yours. Architects have tried very different answers.

cards.headline: What counts as a slum?
cards.body: UN-Habitat counts a household as a slum household if it lacks one or more of five things: durable housing, enough living space, improved water, improved sanitation, or secure tenure (the right to stay). Informal settlements are areas where residents lack that secure tenure, basic services are often missing, and homes may not meet planning and building rules. A roof isn't enough. You also need the right to keep it.

cards.headline: A palace for tenants
cards.body: One answer is for the city to build. Vienna's Karl-Marx-Hof, designed by Karl Ehn in the Red Vienna social housing era (1919 to 1934), is about 1,100 meters long and originally held 1,382 apartments. Yet only about 18% of its site was built on. The rest is courtyards and green space, alongside laundries, baths and kindergartens. A very long building, wrapped around a lot of garden.

mascot.line: Half a house in the right place can beat a whole house in the wrong one.

cards.headline: Half of a good house
cards.body: Another answer: build half, and let families finish it. Alejandro Aravena's firm ELEMENTAL designs social housing it calls "half of a good house," leaving room for residents to finish their homes themselves. According to the Pritzker Prize, this "incremental housing" lets social housing be built on more expensive land, closer to jobs and opportunity. Aravena won the 2016 Pritzker Architecture Prize.

title: Planned Capitals
objective: After this level you can describe planned capitals like Brasília and Washington.
summary: Washington was chosen by law (1790) and drawn by L'Enfant (1791): diagonals over a grid, the Capitol on a 'pedestal'. Brasília (1960) opened the interior; UNESCO praised it, critics didn't.

cards.headline: Some capitals were drawn on paper before a single street existed.
cards.body: In 1790, the Residence Act let President George Washington choose the site of a brand-new national capital. The city had to be invented from scratch, on paper first.

cards.headline: Diagonals over a grid
cards.body: Pierre L'Enfant's 1791 plan laid diagonal avenues radiating from the Capitol across a grid of streets, with circles, squares and parks where the avenues meet. It's Level 82's grid with shortcuts slashed across it. He put the Capitol on Jenkins' Hill, a site he called "a pedestal waiting for a monument."

cards.fact: The planner who wouldn't draw.
cards.context: L'Enfant refused to produce drawings for the Capitol, saying he carried the design "in his head," and he was dismissed in 1792. Level 1 said an architect's job ends in drawings builders can work from. A design in your head is a design nobody else can build.

cards.headline: A capital in the interior
cards.body: Brasília was built to promote settlement and development of Brazil's interior; the government began moving there from Rio de Janeiro on 21 April 1960. Lúcio Costa's plan is often compared to an airplane or a bird: a straight Monumental Axis for government buildings, crossed by a curved Highway Axis of homes. Oscar Niemeyer designed its landmark buildings.

cards.headline: Praised and criticized
cards.body: UNESCO listed Brasília as World Heritage in 1987 for its unique plan and architecture. Critics attacked its cost and architecture, and the writer Simone de Beauvoir found its housing districts sterile. A planned capital gets judged twice: once as a drawing, and again by the people who live in it.

title: Checkpoint: Cities
objective: After this level you can explain how streets, walls, parks and transport shape a city.
summary: Barcelona tore down its walls and Cerdà spread a chamfered grid, with gardens in each block, over the old field of fire. Speculators filled the gardens; Cerdà gave us the word urbanization.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: the man who redrew Barcelona invented the word urbanization.
cards.body: Ildefons Cerdà is credited with coining it, in his General Theory of Urbanization (1867). His Barcelona pulls this whole chapter together: walls, grids, squares, gardens and traffic.

cards.headline: Walls down, grid out
cards.body: Barcelona's new district, the Eixample, was built on open land left clear to give a field of fire from the city walls. Level 83 showed walls cramping growing cities. In 1859, the engineer Ildefons Cerdà drew up a grid plan to extend Barcelona beyond its old walls, and it won royal approval. Level 82's grid, laid over the old killing ground.

mascot.line: Look at Barcelona from above: all those clipped corners are Cerdà's.

cards.headline: Corners cut, gardens planned
cards.body: Cerdà cut the corners of his blocks at 45 degrees so traffic could see along the crossing streets. Every crossing became a small open space, a bit like Level 85's squares. His blocks were also meant to leave open space and gardens in the middle, Level 84's idea of green for everyone, tucked inside every block.

cards.fact: Then the gardens filled up.
cards.context: The plan was not fully carried out: within 30 years the open areas had been built over and building density tripled. Birkenhead's houses paid for its park; in Barcelona, the buildings won and the gardens lost. A plan is a promise, and every city decides how much of it to keep.

title: Green Buildings
objective: After this level you can explain how buildings can save energy.
summary: The first Passive House (Darmstadt, 1991) keeps heat in with insulation, good windows and airtightness. Overhangs admit winter sun. Heat recovery swaps air but keeps the warmth.

cards.headline: In 1991, four families moved into a house that barely needs heating.
cards.body: The row of four homes in Darmstadt, Germany, was the world's first Passive House, and the family of Wolfgang Feist, who developed the idea, lived in one of them. The trick is three plain ideas: keep the heat in, let the sun help, and never throw warm air away.

cards.headline: Wrap it like a flask
cards.body: The Passive House Institute lists five principles: very good insulation, highly energy-efficient windows, airtightness, no thermal bridges, and ventilation with heat recovery. The Darmstadt pioneers even had triple-glazed windows made specially for the job. Here's an analogy: a vacuum flask keeps tea hot for hours without heating it at all. It simply lets almost nothing escape.

cards.headline: Let the sun do some of the work
cards.body: Passive solar design uses the building itself, its windows, walls and floors, to collect and store the sun's heat. The US Department of Energy advises main windows facing within 30 degrees of true south. Then a roof overhang does something clever. The high summer sun hits the overhang and leaves the window in shade; the low winter sun slips underneath and warms the room. Heavy floors and walls, called thermal mass, store that warmth.

cards.fact: Fresh air, without throwing the heat away.
cards.context: An airtight house still has to breathe. A heat recovery ventilator sends stale air out and fresh air in through a heat exchanger, where heat moves from the warmer stream to the cooler one. In winter, the warm air leaving your house warms the cold air coming in; in summer it works the other way round. The Darmstadt homes had four ventilation units doing exactly this.

title: Living Walls
objective: After this level you can explain green roofs and planted walls.
summary: Green roofs come light (extensive) or heavy (intensive, with trees). Patrick Blanc's walls grow on felt with no soil. Milan's Vertical Forest holds 800 trees, tied down against the wind.

cards.headline: Two towers in Milan hold 800 trees on their balconies.
cards.body: Stefano Boeri's Vertical Forest, built from 2007 to 2014, packs greenery equal to about five hectares of parkland onto two apartment towers. Planting a building is harder than it sounds. Soil is heavy, and a tree high up has to stand up to the wind.

cards.headline: Two kinds of green roof
cards.body: A green roof is a layer of plants grown on a rooftop, and it comes in two weights. An extensive roof uses hardy plants in just 2 to 4 inches of growing medium: light, and needing little care. An intensive roof can be a whole park with trees, and it's heavier, so the building needs more structural support. Both earn their keep: their surfaces stay cooler than an ordinary roof, and they reduce and filter the rainwater running off it.

cards.headline: A garden with no soil
cards.body: The botanist Patrick Blanc grows his living walls without any soil. A metal frame holds a 1 cm sheet of PVC, and on that goes a layer of felt. Plant roots grow on and inside the felt, and water with added nutrients trickles down from the top. The whole thing, plants and frame included, weighs under 30 kg per square metre, so it can go on any wall. One covers the Quai Branly museum in Paris, completed in 2004.

cards.fact: Milan's trees wear seatbelts.
cards.context: Level 2 said wind is a live load that pushes sideways, and a tree on a balcony catches plenty of it. The engineers at Arup ran two wind tunnel test campaigns. title: Tall Timber
objective: After this level you can explain how new wood products allow wooden high-rises.
summary: Cross-laminated timber glues boards in crossing layers, making stiff panels. Thick timber chars slowly, insulating its core. Ascent in Milwaukee (CTBUH, 2022) mixes mass timber with concrete.

cards.headline: In 2022, a 25-story tower was named the world's tallest timber building.
cards.body: The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH) certified Ascent, in Milwaukee, at 86.6 meters. Remember Level 6: after the fire of 1666, London rebuilt in brick for protection from fire. So how does a wooden high-rise make sense?

cards.headline: Boards, crossed and glued
cards.body: The key product is cross-laminated timber, or CLT: layers of lumber boards stacked crosswise, typically at right angles, and glued together, at least three layers thick. It was introduced in the early 1990s in Austria and Germany. Crossing the layers is the whole point. A crossed panel is stable, strong and stiff in both directions, so it can make wide floor slabs and whole walls. Here's an analogy: a woven mat holds together far better than a pile of loose straws.

cards.headline: Why a thick timber survives a fire
cards.body: Wood burns, but thick wood burns slowly and predictably. Fire turns its surface to char, and that char insulates the wood inside, slowing the damage. In a standard fire test, wood chars at an average of about 0.6 mm per minute. A timber's strength depends on how much solid wood is left, so a thick one keeps much of its strength while its outside burns away. Here's an analogy: a big log on a campfire, black outside, solid inside.

mascot.line: London swapped wood for brick. Milwaukee brought wood back, and tested it in fire first.

cards.fact: Ascent's timber stands on concrete.
cards.context: Ascent is a hybrid. Its base and its elevator and stair shafts are concrete; 19 of its 25 stories are mass timber, built from CLT and glulam. Before it rose, the USDA Forest Products Laboratory worked with its designers to test how a three-hour fire would affect its glulam columns. Level 6 said wood is strong for its weight; tall timber puts that strength to work, and plans for the fire.

title: 3D-Printed Houses
objective: After this level you can explain how houses can be printed layer by layer.
summary: A concrete printer builds walls layer by layer with no formwork. The mix must flow, then carry the layers above. Steel reinforcement is hard to add. Eindhoven's first printed home got tenants in 2021.

cards.headline: On 30 April 2021, a couple got the keys to a house shaped like a boulder.
cards.body: It was the first 3D-printed concrete home in the Netherlands, in Eindhoven, and it met all of the country's strict building rules. Nobody poured its walls into a mold. A machine built them up, layer by layer.

cards.headline: No mold needed
cards.body: Ordinary concrete needs formwork: a temporary structure that holds the wet mix in shape until it hardens. It's the concrete cousin of Level 4's centering, the wooden frame that holds up an arch until the keystone is set. Formwork can take more than half the resources of a concrete structure. A construction printer skips it. Following a digital design, it squeezes concrete through a nozzle and builds the wall layer by layer.

cards.headline: Runny enough to squeeze, stiff enough to stack
cards.body: That makes the mix a balancing act. It has to flow well enough to push through the nozzle, then be strong enough to carry the weight of every layer printed on top of it without deforming. Engineers call this buildability. Here's an analogy: toothpaste that slides out of the tube but keeps its shape on the brush.

cards.fact: Printing still has Level 7's problem.
cards.context: Concrete is weak when stretched, so builders usually cast steel bars inside to take the tension. In a printed wall that's hard: building layer by layer makes conventional steel reinforcement difficult to add, and the joints between layers are weaker than solid cast concrete. The Eindhoven house was printed as 24 separate elements in a factory, then trucked to the site and set on a foundation.

title: Floating Buildings
objective: After this level you can explain how buildings can float on water.
summary: A floating house sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does. Maasbommel's amphibious houses sit on hollow concrete bases and rise on mooring posts; in 2011 they floated.

cards.headline: In 2011, a Dutch river rose, and the houses on its banks rose with it.
cards.body: At Maasbommel in the Netherlands, 32 amphibious houses and 14 floating ones were built in 2004 and 2005 outside the river dikes. In 2011 the River Maas rose high enough for the amphibious houses to float for the first time. No problems were found. So how does a house built on concrete float?

cards.headline: Archimedes moves in
cards.body: A floating object sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does; then the water's upward push holds it up. That's why a lump of clay sinks but the same clay shaped into a boat floats, and why steel ships float too. Shape does the work. So each amphibious house at Maasbommel stands on a large, hollow concrete cube: plenty of room to push water aside.

title: Building on the Moon
objective: After this level you can explain plans for bases on the Moon.
summary: The Moon has no shielding air and wild temperature swings. A pressurized habitat is mainly in tension. ESA's 2013 study proposed a printed regolith catenary dome over an inflatable.

cards.headline: On the Moon, the biggest push on a building comes from inside it.
cards.body: A Moon base has to hold Earth-level air pressure where there's no atmosphere outside. That outward push is several orders of magnitude bigger than the gravity and weather loads on buildings on Earth. It turns Chapter 1's rules inside out.

cards.headline: A tough building site
cards.body: The Moon has only a very thin atmosphere, so nothing blocks the Sun's radiation or incoming meteoroids. In full sunlight its surface reaches about 127 °C; in darkness it drops to about -173 °C. That's a swing of about 300 degrees between sunlight and shadow. Gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, so everything weighs less, but that's the only easy part.

cards.headline: The inside-out building
cards.body: On Earth, gravity squeezes buildings: Level 2's compression. A pressurized Moon habitat is mainly in tension instead, its walls pushed outward and stretched by the air inside. Here's an analogy: a balloon's skin, pulled tight by the air it holds. To protect it, engineers suggest a thick outer layer of regolith, the Moon's loose, broken soil and rock, to dampen temperature swings and shield against radiation.

mascot.line: Hooke's hanging chain, from 1675 all the way to the Moon. Good ideas travel well.

cards.fact: In 2013, ESA tested printing a Moon base from Moon soil.
cards.context: ESA and partners including the architects Foster + Partners studied whether a 3D printer could build a lunar base from regolith. The design: an inflatable, pressurized dome to shelter astronauts, covered by a robot-printed regolith shell. The shell was a weight-bearing catenary dome with hollow, closed cells like bird bones. A catenary is a hanging chain's curve: flip it and you get Level 10's arch. The team printed a 1.5-tonne demonstration block. It was a study, not a base.

title: Saving Old Buildings
objective: After this level you can explain how historic buildings are preserved.
summary: Viollet-le-Duc restored and added; Morris's SPAB (1877) urged protection instead. After the 2019 fire, his Notre-Dame spire was copied exactly. Tate Modern gave a power station a new job.

cards.headline: On 15 April 2019, fire brought down Notre-Dame's spire. Who had designed it?
cards.body: The blaze in Paris destroyed most of the roof, some of the rib vaulting and the spire, a 19th-century addition by the architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, who was appointed to restore the cathedral. Rebuilding it meant taking a side in an old argument about how to save a building.

points: Restored Notre-Dame with Lassus from 1844
Often added new elements of his own design
20th-century critics: that obscured the original

items.label: William Morris and the SPAB
points: Morris wrote its 1877 manifesto with Philip Webb and others
"Put Protection in the place of Restoration"
"Stave off decay by daily care"

cards.headline: Notre-Dame chose the copy
cards.body: Its new timber spire, topped by a metal cross, rose again to 96 m, an exact replica of the one Viollet-le-Duc built in 1859. Carpenters cut and carved it in their workshops, then assembled it piece by piece inside the cathedral, which reopened in December 2024. So the restorer whose additions critics once attacked had his own addition restored, exactly.

mascot.line: Copy it, mend it, or give it a new life? Every old building makes somebody choose.

cards.fact: Sometimes saving a building means giving it a new job.
cards.context: Giles Gilbert Scott's Bankside Power Station in London opened in 1962 and shut down in 1981. Its machinery was removed, and the architects Herzog & de Meuron converted it into an art museum. It opened as Tate Modern on 11 May 2000, and its vast Turbine Hall now holds giant artworks.

title: Design for Everyone
objective: After this level you can explain how buildings are made usable for everyone.
summary: Curb cuts, won by disabled activists, help everyone. Universal design means usable by all people without special adaptation. US rules cap ramps at 1:12.

cards.headline: In 1972, Berkeley cut a slope into one curb. Then everyone used it.
cards.body: Pressed by disabled activists, the city installed its first official curb cut at an intersection on Telegraph Avenue. (The very first curb cuts had appeared in Kalamazoo, Michigan, in 1945.) Then parents with strollers, workers pushing heavy carts and travelers wheeling luggage headed for them too.

cards.headline: Designed for all, from the start
cards.body: The architect Ronald Mace coined a name for that way of thinking: universal design. NC State's Center for Universal Design, founded in 1989 under his guidance, defines it as design usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design. Its seven principles, published in 1997, start with Equitable Use: the same way of using a place for everyone, identical whenever possible, with nobody singled out.

cards.headline: The one-in-twelve rule
cards.body: Some of it is plain arithmetic. The 2010 ADA Standards, the US accessibility rules, say a ramp run can be no steeper than 1:12: every inch of rise needs at least 12 inches of ramp. So a 6-inch step becomes a 6-foot ramp. Try it in your head with the front steps of your home.

cards.fact: Commodity, for everyone.
cards.context: Level 1's Vitruvius said good building needs commodity: usefulness to the people who use it. Universal design asks which people, and answers: all of them, as far as possible, without special adaptations. The curb cut shows why it pays. Built for wheelchair users, it helps parents with strollers, workers with carts and travelers with suitcases too.

title: How to Look at a Building
objective: After this level you can use a simple method to read any building.
summary: Read a building in three steps: stand back and ask what it is for; find how it stands; read its changes, then ask what delights you. Firmness, commodity, delight still works.

cards.headline: That bricked-up window on an old building is a clue.
cards.body: Historic England's guide to recording buildings tells investigators to note blocked doorways, windows and fireplaces, along with joints in the masonry. Buildings change, and they keep the evidence. Here's a simple way to read any building, using Chapter 1 and this one.

cards.headline: Step 1: Stand back
cards.body: Start with a quick overview, Historic England advises: work out what the building is for and its main phases, so you see it as a working whole, not a pile of parts. Ask what it tells you about its origins, form, function, date and development. What it's for is Level 1's commodity: usefulness to the people who use it.

cards.headline: Step 2: Find how it stands
cards.body: Next, ask how it stands. Do thick walls carry the floors, or does a frame? A wall of glass is a giveaway: in a frame building, a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall bears only its own weight (Level 8). Spot an arch? Look for the massive supports resisting its outward thrust (Level 4).

mascot.line: Once you start spotting bricked-up windows, you can't stop. Consider yourself warned.

cards.headline: Step 3: Read the changes, then enjoy it
cards.body: Then look for the story. Historic England's clues to a building's phases include masonry joints, architectural styles, the plan, decoration, and fixtures and fittings. A seam where the stonework or brickwork changes may mark a later addition. Finally, ask what delights you. Firmness, commodity, delight: Vitruvius's three conditions still make a fine checklist.
